scope: Primary sources and supporting implementations from the three-agent research review.

entries.title: Neural Linguistic Steganography
entries.why: Direct prior art for our pretrained language model plus arithmetic coding. Explains how secret bits drive token choices and how the receiver reconstructs those choices from shared probabilities.
entries.caveat: A foundational construction, not evidence that our finite framing, candidate filtering, or numerical runtime preserves the original model distribution.

entries.title: Near-imperceptible Neural Linguistic Steganography via Self-Adjusting Arithmetic Coding
entries.why: Historical follow-up on arithmetic coding that adapts coding decisions to improve the capacity and distribution-distortion tradeoff.
entries.caveat: Supporting reference discovered during the survey. Near-imperceptibility and favorable measured KL divergence should not be treated as an audited end-to-end security guarantee.

entries.title: Provably Secure Generative Linguistic Steganography (ADG)
entries.status: Findings of ACL-IJCNLP 2021; arXiv author copy
entries.why: An influential method that recursively groups candidate tokens to carry message bits. Useful for understanding why grouping methods can sacrifice capacity.
entries.caveat: Later work qualifies exact distribution-preservation claims: arbitrary discrete probabilities cannot generally be partitioned into perfectly equal-probability groups.

entries.title: Meteor: Cryptographically Secure Steganography for Realistic Distributions
entries.why: Establishes cryptographic treatment of generative steganography when token entropy varies widely. Relevant to shared randomness, security definitions, and why ordinary arithmetic coding needs careful analysis. Includes historical mobile measurements.
entries.caveat: Its guarantee is relative to the agreed generative model. Historical mobile experiments do not validate our current quantized 3B model or phone-to-desktop interoperability.

entries.title: Discop: Provably Secure Steganography in Practice Based on Distribution Copies
entries.status: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2023; author-hosted PDF
entries.why: An important distribution-preserving baseline using copies of the token distribution. Its recursive variant improves capacity and appears in many later comparisons.
entries.caveat: Requires synchronized sampling and inference. A secure token-level sampler alone does not resolve ambiguous detokenization or message framing.

entries.title: Perfectly Secure Steganography Using Minimum Entropy Coupling
entries.why: Provides the coupling formulation: preserving the cover distribution while maximizing information about the message. Useful theoretical reference for the entropy limit and alternatives to interval coding.
entries.caveat: Exact minimum-entropy coupling is computationally hard. Practical approximations and their decoding behavior must be distinguished from the ideal optimization.

entries.title: Computing Low-Entropy Couplings for Large-Support Distributions (ARIMEC)
entries.why: Extends practical minimum-entropy coupling to large, autoregressive distributions. Relevant when investigating structured message priors and information-efficient encoding.
entries.caveat: A research alternative with different computation and message-distribution assumptions. It is not a replacement for authenticated encryption.

entries.title: Provably Secure Disambiguating Neural Linguistic Steganography (SyncPool)
entries.status: IEEE TDSC, online 2024; often cited as 2025; arXiv author copy
entries.why: Directly addresses our visible-text requirement. Groups prefix-ambiguous token pieces and uses synchronized cryptographic randomness within groups, preserving the token distribution while allowing decoding.
entries.caveat: The within-group randomness carries no payload, so disambiguation can reduce usable capacity. Exact token synchronization still depends on matched inference and shared state.

entries.title: A High-Capacity and Secure Disambiguation Algorithm for Neural Linguistic Steganography (Look-ahead Sync)
entries.why: Retains distinguishable future token paths instead of immediately discarding prefix-overlapping candidates. On Llama3-8B, IMDB, top-k 128 with Discop, reports 2.66 bits/token versus SyncPool's 0.95.
entries.caveat: The same setting produces about 0.42 tokens per model call, or 2.38 calls per token. Capacity gains can increase latency. No author implementation was established during the review; theoretical assumptions deserve separate evaluation.

entries.title: SparSamp: Efficient Provably Secure Steganography Based on Sparse Sampling
entries.why: Strong modern baseline combining distribution preservation with low sampling overhead. In the RRC paper's matched Llama-2-7B comparison it reaches 3.38 bits/token and is faster than RRC.
entries.caveat: Headline token rates do not include a universal solution to tokenization ambiguity. Compare identical distributions and full transmitted bytes before inferring gains for our POC.

entries.title: STEAD: Robust Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography with Diffusion Language Model
entries.why: Explores resistance to token insertion, deletion, and substitution using diffusion language models and error correction. Relevant if the channel must tolerate edited cover text.
entries.caveat: A different model architecture and channel objective from our autoregressive Llama POC. Robustness claims are limited to the evaluated attacks and settings.

entries.title: StegoZip: Enhancing Linguistic Steganography Payload in Practice with Large Language Models
entries.why: Targets our expansion problem by compressing the secret before embedding. Reports about 2.5 times the payload using semantic pruning, rank-based compression, and explicit corrections for restoration errors.
entries.caveat: Uses a trained restoration model; main experiments involve larger models, with a 3B ablation. Reported semantic fidelity metrics do not replace our requirement to check exact bytes, Unicode, and whitespace.

entries.title: Addressing Tokenization Inconsistency in Steganography and Watermarking Based on Large Language Models
entries.why: A direct implementation candidate: filters token choices whose detokenization and retokenization would diverge. Could retain more useful choices than our broad prefix-free filtering. The official Consistency repository includes roundtrip experiments.
entries.caveat: Filtering changes the reference distribution. Its correctness argument does not remove numerical discrepancies between sender and receiver runtimes.

entries.title: Provable Secure Steganography Based on Adaptive Dynamic Sampling
entries.why: Investigates a model API that accepts a seed without exposing full probabilities. Relevant if we want to work through a constrained serving API rather than a custom logits interface.
entries.caveat: The API must reproduce samples for supplied seeds. The authors identify provider nondeterminism as a limitation, so this does not eliminate the need for controlled execution.

entries.title: Breaking the Generative Steganography Trilemma: ANStega for Optimal Capacity, Efficiency, and Security
entries.why: Near-entropy streaming ANS with cryptographic masking and low coding overhead. Particularly relevant to our size target: reports 3.69 bits/token on Qwen2.5-3B and 4.67 on Phi-2 2.7B in its full-vocabulary experiments.
entries.caveat: The decoder consumes the embedder's final ANS state. Transporting or reconstructing that state must be accounted for before treating this as a self-contained cover-text protocol. Numerical compatibility remains necessary.

entries.title: HiTMS: A High-Throughput Multi-Stream Linguistic Steganography Framework
entries.why: Adds framing and scheduling for multiple batched cover streams. Reports up to 4.3 times throughput. Its implementation includes Llama3.2-3B, making it relevant to our current model choice.
entries.caveat: Throughput gains do not imply shorter total cover. Its protocol-utilization metric must not be confused with entropy utilization. The CUDA implementation and matching batch schedule are not evidence of mobile interoperability.

entries.title: Provably Secure Steganography Based on List Decoding
entries.why: Keeps candidate messages across tokens and resolves ambiguity with a suffix. Useful as an alternative way to approach the available entropy when instantaneous token choices carry little information.
entries.caveat: Needs message length, can maintain up to 2^20 candidates, and allows a small failure probability. A research agent flagged a possible weighted-to-unweighted inequality issue in the capacity argument; this concern was not independently audited. Treat the bound as an author claim pending review.

entries.title: OD-Stega: LLM-Based Relatively Secure Steganography via Optimized Distributions
entries.why: Optimizes the available token entropy subject to a KL or total-variation divergence budget. Addresses a separate bottleneck from coding efficiency and gives a principled alternative to choosing temperature by trial and error.
entries.caveat: A nonzero divergence budget deliberately changes the original sampling distribution. Higher capacity must be evaluated against text quality and detectability.

entries.title: ReTokSync: Self-Synchronizing Tokenization Disambiguation for Generative Linguistic Steganography
entries.why: Resets generation state to the receiver's retokenized view when ambiguity occurs, limiting cascading errors. Promising for retaining capacity with little runtime overhead.
entries.caveat: Above 99.7% accuracy refers to bits, not complete messages. Its evaluated 100% recovery uses additional correction covers through a reliable auxiliary channel. It is not yet our one-cover exact-recovery requirement.

entries.title: Efficient Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography via Range Coding (RRC)
entries.why: A leading direct comparison for our interval coder. Reports approximately 100% entropy utilization and 3.57 bits/token on Llama-2-7B. Its repository documents precision, termination, and tokenization failures that matter for a real text-only protocol.
entries.caveat: Utilization is supported empirically, not by a rigorous optimality proof. Message length is agreed in advance. Repository tests report 100% recovery from token IDs but about 91% from retokenized text for one 128-bit setting, and require matched inference environments.

entries.title: Linguistic Steganography via Self-Adjusting Asymmetric Number System
entries.why: Another modern ANS-based approach, with adaptive candidate selection and user-selected embedding rates. Useful for comparing capacity, generation quality, and coding overhead.
entries.caveat: Keep its rate and distortion definitions separate from claims of exact preservation of an unmodified model distribution. It is a distinct method from ANStega.

entries.title: A Comprehensive Survey on Linguistic Steganography: Methods, Countermeasures, Evaluation, and Challenges
entries.status: August 2026 arXiv survey; authors report EMNLP 2026 acceptance
entries.why: Map of the field, including 148 steganographic methods, tokenization fixes, evaluation metrics, and engineering limitations. Useful starting point and bibliography for continuing this research.
entries.caveat: A survey indexes claims rather than independently validating every method. Return to the primary papers for security assumptions, exact recovery requirements, and comparable capacity measurements.

entries.title: TE-CSA: trajectory entropy-aware cross-step aggregation for improving embedding capacity of distribution-preserving linguistic steganography
entries.why: Recent diffusion-model extension that aggregates embedding opportunities across denoising steps. Reports 1.84 bits/token versus 0.09 for its architecture-matched timestep-local baseline.
entries.caveat: Its preservation claim assumes a distribution-preserving underlying embedding mechanism. It is a different architecture from our autoregressive POC, and its relative gains cannot be applied to our byte expansion.

entries.title: From Symmetry toward Weak Asymmetry: Secure Steganography under the Receiver's Partial Channel Knowledge
entries.why: Allows receiver-side information such as token rankings instead of exact probability values. Directly relevant to numerical mismatches and eventual decoding across different devices.
entries.caveat: Decoding still depends on the required partial information staying consistent. Precision-mismatch experiments are evidence for that setting, not proof of arbitrary phone-to-desktop compatibility.

entries.title: Independent Meteor CLI
entries.status: Repository documentation snapshot; not independently reproduced
entries.why: An unofficial small-model implementation using LiquidAI LFM2.5-230M-Base. Relevant to packaging and reducing inference requirements.
entries.caveat: Separate from the original Meteor paper's artifact. No convincing cross-device or phone benchmark was established in this review; retain upstream licensing information.

entries.title: Perniciosa Vulpis
entries.status: Repository documentation snapshot; not independently reproduced
entries.why: Independent C/C++ Meteor-style library using pinned llama.cpp and Llama3.2 1B/3B GGUF models. Closely related to our local-model deployment and visible-text synchronization requirements.
entries.caveat: The reviewed deterministic profile targets x86-64. The displayed 7.211 bits/token example uses a mock backend, not Llama. Documentation was reviewed; code was not run.

entries.title: StegText Framework
entries.status: Repository documentation snapshot; not independently reproduced
entries.why: Comparison harness exposing several coders and disambiguators, with a Qwen2.5-3B CUDA quickstart. Useful for controlled experiments rather than reimplementing every baseline.
entries.caveat: Repository claims were not reproduced. Author provenance and equivalence of every algorithm implementation were not independently established.

entries.title: Awesome Linguistic Steganography
entries.status: Repository documentation snapshot; not independently reproduced
entries.why: The survey authors' curated source list, useful for finding papers beyond the primary sources in this archive.
entries.caveat: A discovery aid, not evidence that listed claims have been reproduced or that every new method is suitable for exact text transport.
